introduction-why-do-we-need-a-strategy.core: Many people changing the same code need shared rules about where work lives and how it joins. A branching strategy is that agreement, and it trades isolation against integration speed.

first_principles.problem: Without a convention, everyone branches and merges differently, conflicts pile up, and nobody knows what's in production.
truths: Parallel changes eventually have to integrate.
The longer branches stay apart, the harder they are to merge.
Release cadence shapes what structure you need.
derivation: Pick a strategy that fits your **release cadence**.

analogy.title: Too many cooks in a kitchen
analogy.story: Ten chefs stirring one pot without talking ruin the soup. Stations and hand-offs keep it edible.
analogy.breaks: Strategy can't replace communication or tests; it only structures them.

example.title: A team with no strategy
example.scenario: Feature branches that live for months.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Integration pain grows with how long branches live.

example.outcome: the team shares one integration model.

check.q: What core trade-off does a branching strategy balance?
check.a: Isolation of work-in-progress against speed and frequency of integration.

gitflow-the-classic-structured-approach.core: GitFlow uses main (released code), develop (integration), plus feature, release and hotfix branches. It suits scheduled, versioned releases but is heavy for continuous delivery.

first_principles.problem: Projects that ship versions on fixed dates need a place to stabilise a release while new work continues.
truths: Versioned products have to support release stabilisation.
Hotfixes must reach production without unreleased work.
More branch types bring more overhead.
derivation: **feature/*** off develop; **release/*** to stabilise; **hotfix/*** off main.

analogy.title: A publishing house
analogy.story: Manuscripts (features) go to the editor's desk (develop), a print run is frozen for proofing (release), and errata go out on printed books (hotfix).
analogy.breaks: For apps that deploy many times a day, the long-lived develop branch just adds delay.

example.title: Shipping v2.0 on a date
example.outcome: releases are stable and new work isn't blocked.

check.q: Why are hotfixes merged into both main and develop?
check.a: So the fix ships now and isn't lost from the next release.

github-flow-simple-and-continuous.core: GitHub Flow has one rule: main is always deployable. Branch, open a PR, review, merge, deploy. It fits web apps that ship continuously.

first_principles.problem: Five branch types are overkill when you deploy several times a day.
truths: Frequent deploys need a simple model.
Code review is the main quality gate.
Small changes are low risk.
derivation: Open a **PR**, get CI and review.

analogy.title: A food truck's single menu board
analogy.story: One board, always accurate. Change one item, check it, and put it up.
analogy.breaks: It doesn't handle maintaining several released versions at once.

example.title: A SaaS bug fix
example.scenario: From branch to production in an hour.

check.q: What is GitHub Flow's one key rule?
check.a: Anything on main is always deployable.

trunk-based-development-tbd.core: In trunk-based development, everyone integrates into main at least daily through tiny, short-lived branches (or directly). Incomplete work is hidden behind flags.

first_principles.problem: Even PR branches that live a week accumulate conflicts and delay feedback.
truths: Merge pain grows with the size of the divergence.
Continuous integration means integrating continuously.
Strong automated tests make frequent merges safe.

analogy.title: Zipping a jacket as you go
analogy.story: Zip a little at a time and it never jams. Try to zip two misaligned halves all at once and it does.
analogy.breaks: It requires disciplined testing and flags. Without them, trunk breaks constantly.

example.title: A feature built over two weeks
example.scenario: Ten small merges instead of one big one.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: No big-bang merge, and integration bugs show up on day 1.

example.outcome: integration is continuous and conflicts stay tiny.

check.q: How does TBD ship half-finished features safely?
check.a: It merges them behind feature flags that keep them off for users.

tbds-best-friend-feature-flags.core: A feature flag is a runtime switch around code paths. It separates deploying code from releasing a feature, so you can turn features on gradually and roll back instantly.

first_principles.problem: With trunk-based development, unfinished features would otherwise reach production users.
truths: Deploying and releasing are different events.
Configuration can change without a redeploy.
Flags that are never removed become debt.
derivation: **Deploy dark**, then turn it on for a percentage or group.

analogy.title: A light switch wired before the party
analogy.story: The wiring is installed (deployed) days early; you flip the lights on (release) when guests arrive.
analogy.breaks: Too many stale flags create combinatorial complexity and dead code.

steps.label: Rollback
steps.detail: When errors spike at 10%, flip it off in seconds with no deploy.

check.q: What's the main risk of feature flags?
check.a: Accumulating stale flags that add complexity and untested combinations.

the-reality-of-merge-conflicts.core: Conflicts happen when both sides changed the same lines. Git marks them and a human picks the correct result. Small, frequent merges keep them small.

first_principles.problem: Developers fear conflict markers and sometimes resolve them by blindly picking one side, losing work.
truths: Git can't infer intent when both sides edited the same lines.
Conflict size scales with divergence.
Resolution needs understanding both changes.

analogy.title: Two people editing the same sentence
analogy.story: Neither version wins automatically; you rewrite the sentence so it carries both intents.
analogy.breaks: No markers doesn't mean no conflict. Semantic conflicts (renamed function calls) still slip through.

example.title: A config timeout conflict
example.scenario: Both raised it to different values.

steps.label: Resolve
steps.detail: Talk to the author, pick 45, run the tests, commit.

check.q: Why can a clean merge still be broken?
check.a: Semantic conflicts, like a renamed function still called elsewhere, don't produce markers.

monorepo-vs-polyrepo-an-organizational-c.core: A monorepo keeps all code in one repository (atomic cross-project changes, shared tooling). A polyrepo gives each service its own (independence, simpler per-repo tooling). Each choice shifts where the complexity lives.

first_principles.problem: Changing a shared library across 20 polyrepos needs 20 coordinated PRs, while a large monorepo needs serious build tooling.
truths: Code organisation shapes collaboration.
Atomic changes are easier in one place.
Scale needs tooling either way.
derivation: **Monorepo**: one atomic commit across services, shared CI; needs Bazel, Nx and the like.
**Polyrepo**: autonomy and clear ownership; harder cross-cutting changes.
Choose based on **coupling and team structure**.

analogy.title: One big shared house vs. separate apartments
analogy.story: A house makes renovating the plumbing for everyone easy; apartments give privacy but need separate contractors.
analogy.breaks: Neither is universally better. Many organisations use a hybrid.

example.title: Upgrading a logging library

steps.label: Choice
steps.detail: Tightly coupled services favour a monorepo.

example.outcome: repo layout matches how the code is coupled.

check.a: Atomic cross-project changes in a single commit and PR.
